classification.tone: Grounded, emotional, reflective, with light comedic fish-out-of-water texture

evaluation.positioning_hook: A high-powered suburban executive wakes up missing ten years of memory and must rebuild his marriage, family, and conscience before the truth catches him.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean emotional promise: a successful husband and father confronting the life he can’t remember. The hook is accessible and the family/marriage stakes are easy to grasp, though the appeal is more adult-drama than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script establishes its engine quickly: Tim wakes in 2009 believing it is 1999, then discovers his wife, kids, office, and social life have all moved on without his memory. The opening sequence and the doctor visits make the central question very clear.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Tim is built as a likable, status-conscious man whose confusion reveals vulnerability, humor, and regret. Nancy, Steve, Jean, and Josh each give him a different mirror, and the role has strong actor-facing material, though Tim remains the dominant engine.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The memory-loss premise is familiar, but the specific twist of a ten-year gap inside a marriage and career gives it a more adult, emotionally loaded angle. The script leans into recognizable domestic and office rhythms rather than flashy invention, which keeps it accessible.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves through a clear chain of discovery: home, office, bar, doctor, psychologist, library, hypnosis, and finally the triggering memory. The structure keeps the mystery alive, though much of the momentum comes from repeated revelation scenes rather than escalating external action.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a man discovering he has lost a decade of his life lands immediately, and the final reveal that his memory gap is tied to a hit-and-run gives the premise a moral charge. The emotional inevitability is strong even when the execution stays fairly classical.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The suburban home, corporate office, bar culture, medical offices, and library all feel specific to a late-1990s/2009 contrast. The world is not sprawling, but it is textured enough to make the time-jump disorientation tangible and story-generating.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct blend of midlife comedy, marital tension, and existential unease. Tim’s confusion over flat screens, GPS, Bluetooth, and Google gives the piece a recognizable comic texture that sits inside a more serious emotional frame.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the memory mystery is a story about moral drift, emotional absence, and the cost of a life lived on autopilot. The affair, the family fracture, and the eventual hit-and-run reveal suggest deeper thematic layers that reward a patient audience.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Tim/Nancy is the core relationship, but Steve, Jean, Jacob, Julie, Josh, and Stephanie each create a different pressure point around him. The ensemble is functional and scene-generating, though the script still lives primarily through Tim’s point of view.

casting_characteristics: Male lead in late 30s/40s playing a man who ages into his late 40s/50s
Female lead in 30s/40s playing wife across a decade span
Teen daughter and 10-year-old son in early scenes
Adult versions of children and a grandson in later scenes
Supporting roles for office, medical, and bar environments

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with some suburban exterior and parking-garage work
notable_requirements: Corporate office floor and executive office

technical.vfx_details: No visible VFX requirement beyond simple title/date inserts and possible flashback transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: Minimal practical needs; a bicycle impact and car backing incident are the key physical beats.

rights_flags.detail: Bradley Cooper is referenced by name in a TV segment.
Oldies 104.7, Def Leppard, and a quoted song lyric/line are referenced.
Sham-Wow, Google, XM Radio, GPS, Rogaine, Perrier, Evian, Land Rover, Porsche, L.A. Kings, and other consumer brands are named.
The script references 'Mister Rogers' style language and a 'Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood' refrain, which may invite clearance review depending on usage.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Theatrical or premium-streaming adult drama lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a festival-to-platform or modest theatrical adult drama with strong word-of-mouth potential.

cost.note: Contemporary domestic and office settings keep the footprint contained, with only modest practical staging for the car and bicycle incident.

cast.note: The project depends on a strong lead and a handful of age-specific family roles, including child and adult versions of the children.

location.note: The story is built from a small number of repeatable interiors and nearby exteriors rather than large-scale travel or set builds.

content.note: Marital infidelity, emotional distress, and a hit-and-run reveal push it into adult territory without moving into explicit content.

rights.note: The script uses several named brands, a real celebrity reference, and a few culturally specific pop references that would need a clearance pass.

strengths.what_it_means: A man waking up ten years ahead of his own life is a clean, high-emotion engine that buyers can understand in one breath. It gives the audience a built-in question, a built-in mystery, and a built-in emotional payoff.
strengths.evidence: Tim wakes in 2009 believing it is 1999, then discovers his wife, children, office, and social status have all changed around him.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Tim is built for an actor.
strengths.what_it_means: The role lets a performer play denial, vanity, confusion, tenderness, embarrassment, and moral awakening in one track. That kind of contradiction is exactly what makes a lead feel castable and memorable.
strengths.evidence: He moves from joking about pizza and golf to panicking over flat screens, GPS, and his own reflection, then later breaks down over his family.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The marriage is the real engine.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not just a memory mystery; it’s a story about a long marriage that has quietly gone stale and then gets a second chance. That gives the script emotional reach beyond the gimmick and makes it attractive to adult audiences.
strengths.evidence: Nancy’s conversations with Tim repeatedly point to years of distance, routine, and resentment, then turn into a fragile reconnection.

strengths.what_it_means: The script gets easy laughs from Tim’s confusion with flat screens, Bluetooth, GPS, Google, and office tech, which keeps the tone buoyant while the emotional stakes deepen. That balance broadens the audience and gives the material a commercial rhythm.
strengths.evidence: Tim struggles with the TV, the coffee maker, the GPS, the internet, and the receptionist’s Bluetooth headset.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The supporting players each sharpen a different angle.
strengths.what_it_means: Steve, Jean, Josh, Nancy, and Stephanie all function as distinct mirrors for Tim’s identity, giving the script a strong scene-to-scene variety. That makes the material attractive to recognizable character actors and keeps the dialogue engine alive.
strengths.evidence: Steve exposes Tim’s affair and work habits; Jean knows him from the beginning; Josh frames the mystery; Nancy carries the marriage; Stephanie embodies the road not taken.

strengths.what_it_means: The final memory of the hit-and-run turns the premise from personal confusion into guilt, consequence, and responsibility. That gives the story a stronger aftertaste than a simple amnesia puzzle.
strengths.evidence: The closing flashback shows Tim backing his SUV into a child on a bicycle and driving away.

strengths.what_it_means: This is a contained contemporary drama with repeatable locations and modest technical demands, which makes it easier to package and finance than a larger-scale mystery. It has the feel of a smart adult feature that can be made without spectacle.
strengths.evidence: Most of the script plays in the house, office, bar, clinic, psychologist office, library, and parking garage.

whats_special.headline: 10 Years Removed is a clean, actor-friendly adult drama with a built-in hook: a successful suburban husband wakes up missing a decade and discovers the life he built has drifted far from the man he used to be. The script pairs accessible time-shift comedy with marriage, guilt, and consequence, ending on a reveal that gives the premise real emotional bite.

lead_characters.name: Tim Sullivan
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 30s to early 40s playing into 50s
lead_characters.hook: Tim is a polished, status-conscious corporate partner whose identity is built on competence, routine, and control until the floor drops out from under him. He’s funny without trying to be, vain without being monstrous, and deeply human in the way he keeps reaching for normalcy even as every object, relationship, and habit around him has changed. The role is a slow-burn emotional unmasking: the man who thinks he’s just having a bad morning becomes the man forced to confront what kind of husband, father, and citizen he’s been.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a showcase part because it gives an actor a full spectrum of playable states: comic confusion, social authority, panic, shame, tenderness, and eventual moral reckoning. It has the same kind of transformation energy that makes roles like Michael Keaton in Birdman or Colin Firth in A Single Man so compelling: a man whose interior life becomes visible through pressure.

lead_characters.name: Nancy Sullivan
lead_characters.hook: Nancy is the emotional ballast of the story: smart, dry, affectionate, and exhausted by years of carrying the marriage’s invisible labor. She is not written as a passive spouse; she has wit, authority, and a lived-in history with Tim that makes every exchange feel earned. Her power comes from the fact that she can needle him, love him, and wound him in the same breath.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role actors pursue when they want to play intelligence and heartbreak without melodrama. It offers the same emotional terrain as Julianne Moore in Still Alice or Frances McDormand in pieces of domestic realism: a woman whose restraint is as expressive as her tears.

lead_characters.name: Steve Johnson
lead_characters.hook: Steve is Tim’s best friend and the script’s pressure valve: loud, crude, loyal, and far more self-aware than he first appears. He’s the guy who can joke about everything, including Tim’s affair, while still functioning as the blunt instrument of truth. He gives the movie its social texture and its male-bonding friction.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy supporting role for an actor who knows how to play charm with rot underneath. It has the same kind of scene-stealing, lived-in energy as a Philip Seymour Hoffman or John C. Reilly type of part: funny, messy, and emotionally useful.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Joshua Strasberg
lead_characters.hook: Josh is the calm, slightly eccentric professional who becomes the story’s guide through memory, denial, and self-recognition. He’s warm, a little theatrical, and smart enough to know when to push and when to let Tim breathe. He gives the film a cerebral counterweight without ever becoming cold.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong character role for an actor who can play intelligence with humanity and a touch of wit. It lives in the same lane as a Paul Giamatti or Stanley Tucci type of performance: authoritative, humane, and quietly memorable.

director_appeal.hook: A director who can make emotional dislocation feel cinematic without losing the humor.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards a filmmaker who likes intimate performance, clean visual storytelling, and tonal control. There’s a real opportunity here to stage ordinary spaces — a kitchen, office, bar, clinic — as places of identity crisis, while letting the final reveal land with emotional force rather than spectacle.

buyer_appeal.lane: Adult drama / prestige indie / streaming original lane
buyer_appeal.detail: This fits a lane that values a strong hook, contained production, and actor-driven storytelling. It does not need a giant cast or heavy effects; it needs a lead with range, a credible supporting ensemble, and a buyer looking for a smart, emotional premise with a clean marketing line.

considerations.area: The premise plays strongest as an adult character drama.
considerations.detail: The hook is commercial, but the emotional center is intimate and reflective, so the cleanest positioning is for audiences who respond to relationship-driven mystery rather than high-concept spectacle.

considerations.area: The opening and middle sections repeat a similar discovery rhythm.
considerations.detail: A future pass could consider varying the sequence of revelations so each new beat feels like a fresh turn rather than another version of the same shock-and-adjust pattern. The underlying material is strong; the pacing lever is in how the discoveries are spaced.

considerations.area: Tim’s emotional arc is the movie’s spine.
considerations.detail: The script already gives him a compelling transformation, and a next pass could foreground the moments where his new awareness changes how he speaks to Nancy, Steve, and Jacob. That would make the eventual moral reveal hit even harder.

considerations.area: The final reveal reframes the whole story.
considerations.detail: The hit-and-run ending gives the premise a strong moral landing, and the script could continue to protect that reveal as the emotional destination of the piece. It’s the kind of ending that can elevate the project in the room if the earlier scenes are positioned as a gradual path toward accountability.

considerations.area: The brand and pop references are very specific to their moment.
considerations.detail: The script’s texture benefits from the era markers, but a production pass should review which named references are essential to the joke and which can be generalized without losing the effect.
